lesson.title: Trigonal Planar Bonding: sp2 Hybridization
lesson.summary: Three electron domains call for sp2 hybridization, mixing one s orbital and two p orbitals into a flat trio of hybrid orbitals spaced 120 degrees apart, with one pure p orbital left over for pi bonding.
lesson.body:
Moving up from two electron domains to three changes both the hybridization and the geometry. A central atom with three electron domains mixes one s orbital with two of its three p orbitals, producing three sp2 hybrid orbitals. Each carries roughly 33 percent s character and 67 percent p character, and all three point within the same flat plane, spaced exactly 120 degrees apart. This is the orbital-level explanation for trigonal planar geometry: three equivalent regions of electron density spreading out as far from each other as they can while staying in a single plane.

Mixing only two of the three available p orbitals leaves one p orbital untouched. That leftover p orbital is oriented perpendicular to the plane containing the three sp2 orbitals, sticking straight up and down out of the flat sheet of bonds. Like the two leftover p orbitals in sp hybridization, this single leftover p orbital does not participate in sigma bonding, but it becomes essential wherever an sp2 atom needs to form a pi bond as part of a double bond.

Boron trifluoride, BF3, shows sp2 hybridization without any multiple bonds involved. Boron has three valence electrons and forms three single B-F bonds with no lone pairs, giving it three electron domains and sp2 hybridization. The molecule is trigonal planar with F-B-F angles of 120 degrees. Because boron only has three bonds and no lone pair filling out an octet, its leftover, unhybridized p orbital remains completely empty. That empty orbital is the reason BF3 readily accepts an incoming electron pair from other molecules, behaving as a Lewis acid. Formaldehyde, CH2O, is a second everyday sp2 example: its central carbon has three electron domains, one C=O double bond and two C-H single bonds, giving a trigonal planar shape with bond angles close to 120 degrees, built from the same sp2 sigma framework as BF3 plus one additional pi bond across the C=O double bond.

Ethylene, C2H4, shows sp2 hybridization working together with a pi bond. Each carbon in H2C=CH2 has three electron domains, two C-H bonds and one C-C bond, so both carbons are sp2 hybridized. The sp2 orbitals on each carbon form the sigma bonding framework, including the sigma component of the C=C double bond, holding all six atoms in a single flat plane with bond angles close to 120 degrees. The leftover p orbital on each carbon, standing perpendicular to that plane, overlaps sideways with its counterpart on the other carbon to form the pi bond that completes the C=C double bond. Because that pi bond depends on the two p orbitals staying aligned and parallel, ethylene cannot rotate around its C=C bond without breaking that overlap, a restriction explored fully once pi bonds are covered on their own.

The contrast between sp2 and the tetrahedral sp3 case covered next is worth holding onto: sp2 hybridization always leaves exactly one p orbital unhybridized, which is precisely what makes double bonds and trigonal planar geometry go together so consistently. Wherever you see three electron domains and 120 degree angles, whether or not a lone pair or an empty orbital is also present, you can expect sp2 hybridization and, if a multiple bond is drawn, a pi bond built from that single leftover p orbital.
